Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas; where at times, by some infernal trick of legerdemain in the powers of frost and air, he, shivering and half shipwrecked, instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery, views what seems a boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.

Tell me, why this strong young colt, foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont, far removed from all beasts of prey—why is it that upon the sunniest day, if you but shake a fresh buffalo robe behind him, so that he cannot even see it, but only smells its wild animal muskiness—why will he start, snort, and with bursting eyes paw the ground in phrensies of affright? There is no remembrance in him of any gorings of wild creatures in his green northern home, so that the strange muskiness he smells cannot recall to him anything associated with the experience of former perils; for what knows he, this New England colt, of the black bisons of distant Oregon?

No: but here thou beholdest even in a dumb brute, the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, still when he smells that savage musk, the rending, goring bison herds are as present as to the deserted wild foal of the prairies, which this instant they may be trampling into dust.

Thus, then, the muffled rollings of a milky sea; the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains; the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies; all these, to Ishmael, are as the shaking of that buffalo robe to the frightened colt!

Though neither knows where lie the nameless things of which the mystic sign gives forth such hints; yet with me, as with the colt, somewhere those things must exist. Though in many of its aspects this visible world seems formed in love, the invisible spheres were formed in fright.

But not yet have we solved the incantation of this whiteness, and learned why it appeals with such power to the soul; and more strange and far more portentous—why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaning symbol of spiritual things, nay, the very veil of the Christian’s Deity; and yet should be as it is, the intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind.

Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the milky way? Or is it, that as in essence whiteness is not so much a colour as the visible absence of colour; and at the same time the concrete of all colours; is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues—every stately or lovely emblazoning—the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls; all these are but subtile deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from without; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we proceed further, and consider that the mystical cosmetic which produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, for ever remains white or colorless in itself, and if operating without medium upon matter, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge—pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper; and like wilful travellers in Lapland, who refuse to wear coloured and colouring glasses upon their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps all the prospect around him. And of all these things the Albino whale was the symbol. Wonder ye then at the fiery hunt?

Or, to the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the Middle American States, why does the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun, evoke such an eyeless statue in the soul?

Or what is there apart from the traditions of dungeoned warriors and kings (which will not wholly account for it) that makes the White Tower of London tell so much more strongly on the imagination of an untravelled American, than those other storied structures, its neighbors—the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, whence, in peculiar moods, comes that gigantic ghostliness over the soul at the bare mention of that name, while the thought of Virginia’s Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, irrespective of all latitudes and longitudes, does the name of the White Sea exert such a spectralness over the fancy, while that of the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long lacquered mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the gaudiest and yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a wholly unsubstantial instance, purely addressed to the fancy, why, in reading the old fairy tales of Central Europe, does “the tall pale man” of the Hartz forests, whose changeless pallor unrustlingly glides through the green of the groves—why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping imps of the Blocksburg?

Nor is it, altogether, the remembrance of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes; nor the stampedoes of her frantic seas; nor the tearlessness of arid skies that never rain; nor the sight of her wide field of leaning spires, wrenched cope-stones, and crosses all adroop (like canted yards of anchored fleets); and her suburban avenues of house-walls lying over upon each other, as a tossed pack of cards;—it is not these things alone which make tearless Lima, the strangest, saddest city thou can’st see. For Lima has taken the white veil; and there is a higher horror in this whiteness of her woe. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins for ever new; admits not the cheerful greenness of complete decay; spreads over her broken ramparts the rigid pallor of an apoplexy that fixes its own distortions.

I know that, to the common apprehension, this phenomenon of whiteness is not confessed to be the prime agent in exaggerating the terror of objects otherwise terrible; nor to the unimaginative mind is there aught of terror in those appearances whose awfulness to another mind almost solely consists in this one phenomenon, especially when exhibited under any form at all approaching to muteness or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be respectively elucidated by the following examples.

First: The mariner, when drawing nigh the coasts of foreign lands, if by night he hear the roar of breakers, starts to vigilance, and feels just enough of trepidation to sharpen all his faculties; but under precisely similar circumstances, let him be called from his hammock to view his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness—as if from encircling headlands shoals of combed white bears were swimming round him, then he feels a silent, superstitious dread; the shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is horrible to him as a real ghost; in vain the lead assures him he is still off soundings; heart and helm they both go down; he never rests till blue water is under him again. Yet where is the mariner who will tell thee, “Sir, it was not so much the fear of striking hidden rocks, as the fear of that hideous whiteness that so stirred me?”

Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes conveys naught of dread, except, perhaps, in the mere fancying of the eternal frosted desolateness reigning at such vast altitudes, and the natural conceit of what a fearfulness it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same is it with the backwoodsman of the West, who with comparative indifference views an unbounded prairie sheeted with driven snow, no shadow of tree or twig to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas; where at times, by some infernal trick of legerdemain in the powers of frost and air, he, shivering and half shipwrecked, instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery, views what seems a boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But thou sayest, methinks that white-lead chapter about whiteness is but a white flag hung out from a craven soul; thou surrenderest to a hypo, Ishmael.

Tell me, why this strong young colt, foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont, far removed from all beasts of prey—why is it that upon the sunniest day, if you but shake a fresh buffalo robe behind him, so that he cannot even see it, but only smells its wild animal muskiness—why will he start, snort, and with bursting eyes paw the ground in phrensies of affright? There is no remembrance in him of any gorings of wild creatures in his green northern home, so that the strange muskiness he smells cannot recall to him anything associated with the experience of former perils; for what knows he, this New England colt, of the black bisons of distant Oregon?

No: but here thou beholdest even in a dumb brute, the instinct of the knowledge of the demonism in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, still when he smells that savage musk, the rending, goring bison herds are as present as to the deserted wild foal of the prairies, which this instant they may be trampling into dust.

Thus, then, the muffled rollings of a milky sea; the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains; the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies; all these, to Ishmael, are as the shaking of that buffalo robe to the frightened colt!

Though neither knows where lie the nameless things of which the mystic sign gives forth such hints; yet with me, as with the colt, somewhere those things must exist. Though in many of its aspects this visible world seems formed in love, the invisible spheres were formed in fright.

But not yet have we solved the incantation of this whiteness, and learned why it appeals with such power to the soul; and more strange and far more portentous—why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaning symbol of spiritual things, nay, the very veil of the Christian’s Deity; and yet should be as it is, the intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind.

Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the milky way? Or is it, that as in essence whiteness is not so much a colour as the visible absence of colour; and at the same time the concrete of all colours; is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows—a colourless, all-colour of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues—every stately or lovely emblazoning—the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods; yea, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls; all these are but subtile deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from without; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we proceed further, and consider that the mystical cosmetic which produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, for ever remains white or colorless in itself, and if operating without medium upon matter, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge—pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper; and like wilful travellers in Lapland, who refuse to wear coloured and colouring glasses upon their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps all the prospect around him. And of all these things the Albino whale was the symbol. Wonder ye then at the fiery hunt?

modern_en.title: Chapter 42 — The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: What the white whale meant to Ahab has been hinted at. What he was to me, at times, remains unsaid.

Beyond the more obvious fears that Moby Dick could stir in any man's soul, there was another thought — or rather a vague, nameless horror about him — that sometimes overpowered everything else with its intensity. Yet it was so mystical, so nearly impossible to put into words, that I almost despair of making it comprehensible. It was the whiteness of the whale that appalled me above all things. But how can I hope to explain myself here? And yet, in some dim, fumbling way, explain myself I must, or all these chapters will have been for nothing.

In many natural objects, whiteness refines and enhances beauty, as if imparting some special virtue of its own — as in marbles, japonicas, and pearls. Various nations have in some way recognized a certain royal preeminence in this color. The barbaric, grand old kings of Pegu placed the title "Lord of the White Elephants" above all their other grandiloquent titles of dominion. The modern kings of Siam unfurled the same snow-white animal on their royal standard. The Hanoverian flag bore the single figure of a snow-white charger. The great Austrian Empire, Caesarian, heir to overlording Rome, took the same imperial hue for its imperial color. This preeminence applies to the human race itself, giving the white man ideal mastership over every dusky tribe. Beyond all this, whiteness has even been made a sign of gladness — among the Romans, a white stone marked a joyful day. In other human sympathies and symbols, this same color is made the emblem of many touching, noble things: the innocence of brides, the kindliness of old age. Among the Red Men of America, the gift of the white belt of wampum was the deepest pledge of honor. In many lands, whiteness represents the majesty of Justice in the judge's ermine, and adds to the daily grandeur of kings and queens drawn by milk-white steeds. Even in the higher mysteries of the most august religions, it has been made the symbol of divine spotlessness and power. The Persian fire worshippers held the white forked flame the holiest on the altar. In the Greek mythologies, great Jove himself was made incarnate in a snow-white bull. Among the noble Iroquois, the midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog was by far the holiest festival of their theology — that spotless, faithful creature being held the purest envoy they could send to the Great Spirit with the yearly news of their own faithfulness. Directly from the Latin word for white, all Christian priests derive the name of one part of their sacred vestments — the alb, or tunic, worn beneath the cassock. Among the holy ceremonies of the Romish faith, white is specially used in celebrating the Passion of our Lord. In the Vision of St. John, white robes are given to the redeemed, and the twenty-four elders stand clothed in white before the great white throne, and the Holy One who sits there is white like wool. Yet for all these accumulated associations with whatever is sweet, honorable, and sublime, there still lurks something elusive in the innermost idea of this color that strikes more panic into the soul than the redness that frightens us in blood.

It is this elusive quality that causes the thought of whiteness, when separated from kinder associations and joined to any object terrible in itself, to heighten that terror to its furthest limits. Consider the white bear of the poles and the white shark of the tropics. What but their smooth, flaky whiteness makes them the transcendent horrors they are? It is that ghastly whiteness that gives such an abhorrent mildness, even more loathsome than terrifying, to the dumb gloating of their look. So that not even the fierce-fanged tiger in his heraldic coat can so stagger courage as the white-shrouded bear or shark.*

*With reference to the polar bear, it may possibly be argued by anyone who would like to go still deeper into this matter that it is not the whiteness, considered by itself, that heightens the intolerable hideousness of that beast. For, analyzed, that heightened hideousness, it might be said, only arises from the fact that the irresponsible ferociousness of the creature is dressed in the fleece of heavenly innocence and love; and so, by bringing together two such opposite emotions in our minds, the polar bear frightens us with so unnatural a contrast. But even assuming all this to be true, if it were not for the whiteness, you would not have that intensified terror.

As for the white shark, the white gliding ghostliness of that creature at rest, when seen in its ordinary moods, strangely matches the same quality in the polar quadruped. The French hit off this peculiarity most vividly in the name they give that fish. The Romish mass for the dead begins with "Requiem eternam" (eternal rest), from which "Requiem" names the mass itself and any other funeral music. Now, in allusion to the white, silent stillness of death in this shark, and the mild deadliness of his habits, the French call him Requin.

Think of the albatross. Where do those clouds of spiritual wonder and pale dread come from, in which that white phantom sails in every imagination? It was not Coleridge who first cast that spell, but God's great, unflattering poet laureate, Nature.*

*I remember the first albatross I ever saw. It was during a prolonged gale, in waters close to the Antarctic seas. From my morning watch below, I climbed up to the overclouded deck. There, dashed down upon the main hatches, I saw a regal, feathery thing of unspotted whiteness, with a hooked, Roman bill, sublime. At intervals it arched out its vast archangel wings, as if to embrace some holy ark. Wondrous flutterings and throbbings shook it. Though its body was unharmed, it uttered cries like some king's ghost in supernatural distress. Through its inexpressible, strange eyes, I thought I peered into secrets that took hold of God. Like Abraham before the angels, I bowed myself. The white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those forever-exiled waters I had lost the miserable, warping memories of traditions and of towns. Long I gazed at that prodigy of plumage. I cannot tell — I can only hint at — the things that darted through me then. But at last I came to myself, and turning, asked a sailor what bird this was. A goney, he replied. Goney! I had never heard that name before. Is it conceivable that this glorious thing is utterly unknown to men ashore? Never! But some time afterward I learned that "goney" was a seaman's name for the albatross. So by no possibility could Coleridge's wild Rhyme have had anything to do with those mystical impressions of mine when I saw that bird on our deck. For I had not then read the Rhyme, nor did I know the bird to be an albatross. Yet in saying this, I only indirectly polish a little brighter the noble merit of the poem and the poet.

I maintain, then, that the secret of the spell lurks chiefly in the bird's wondrous bodily whiteness. This truth is all the more evident from the fact that, by a contradiction in terms, there are birds called gray albatrosses. These I have often seen, but never with such emotions as when I beheld the Antarctic fowl.

But how had the mystic thing been caught? Don't breathe a word, and I will tell you: with a treacherous hook and line, as the bird floated on the sea. At last the Captain made a postman of it, tying a lettered leather tag around its neck with the ship's time and place, and then letting it escape. But I have no doubt that the leather tag, meant for man, was taken off in Heaven, when the white bird flew up to join the wing-folding, the invoking, and adoring cherubim!

Most famous in our Western annals and Indian traditions is the White Steed of the Prairies — a magnificent milk-white charger, large-eyed, small-headed, broad-chested, with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his lofty, scornful bearing. He was the elected Xerxes of vast herds of wild horses, whose pastures in those days were fenced only by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghenies. At their flaming head he trooped westward like that chosen star which every evening leads on the hosts of light. The flashing cascade of his mane and the curving comet of his tail decked him in trappings more resplendent than gold- and silver-beaters could have furnished. He was a most imperial and archangelic apparition of that unfallen western world, which to the eyes of the old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those primeval times when Adam walked majestic as a god, bluff-browed and fearless as this mighty steed. Whether marching among his aides and marshals at the front of countless columns that streamed endlessly over the plains like an Ohio, or whether, with his subjects browsing all around him to the horizon, he reviewed them at a gallop, his warm nostrils reddening through his cool milkiness — in whatever aspect he presented himself, he was always an object of trembling reverence and awe to the bravest Indians. Nor can it be questioned, from what stands on legendary record of this noble horse, that it was chiefly his spiritual whiteness that so clothed him with divineness; and that this divineness had something in it which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.
But there are other cases where whiteness loses all that added strange glory it possesses in the White Steed and the Albatross.

What is it about the albino man that so particularly repels and often shocks the eye, so that he is sometimes despised by his own family? It is the whiteness that covers him, the very thing expressed by his name. The albino is as well-built as other men — he has no real deformity — and yet this all-pervading whiteness makes him more strangely hideous than the ugliest abortion (a misshapen, monstrous birth). Why should this be?

Nor, in quite different aspects, does Nature, in her least tangible but no less malicious workings, fail to enlist this crowning attribute of the terrible among her forces. From its snowy appearance, the gauntleted ghost of the Southern Seas has been named the White Squall. Nor, in some historical cases, has the art of human malice left out so potent an ally. How wildly it heightens the effect of that passage in Froissart, when, masked in the snowy symbol of their faction, the desperate White Hoods of Ghent murder their bailiff in the marketplace!

In certain things, the common inherited experience of all humanity bears witness to the supernatural quality of this color. It can hardly be doubted that the one visible quality in the appearance of the dead that most horrifies the viewer is the marble paleness lingering there — as if that pallor were as much the mark of terror in the next world as it is of mortal fear in this one. From the pallor of the dead, we borrow the color of the shroud we wrap them in. Even in our superstitions we throw the same snowy cloak around our ghosts — all phantoms rise in a milk-white fog. And while these terrors grip us, let us add that even the king of terrors himself, as portrayed by the evangelist, rides on a pale horse.

Therefore, whatever grand or gracious thing a person may symbolize through whiteness in other moods, no one can deny that in its deepest, most idealized meaning, it summons a peculiar specter to the soul.

But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it would seem impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all direct associations that might lend it anything fearful — is nevertheless found to work the same spell on us, however modified, hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

Let's try. But in a matter like this, subtlety speaks to subtlety, and without imagination nobody can follow anyone else into these halls. And though no doubt at least some of the imaginative impressions I am about to present may have been shared by most people, perhaps few were fully aware of them at the time, and so they may not be able to call them up now.

Why does the bare mention of Whitsuntide (the church season of Pentecost), to the man of untrained imagination who happens to be only loosely acquainted with the particular character of the day, marshal in his fancy such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-pacing pilgrims, downcast and hooded with new-fallen snow? Or why, to the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the Middle American States, does the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun call up such an eyeless statue in the soul?

Or what is it — apart from the traditions of dungeoned warriors and kings, which will not wholly account for it — that makes the White Tower of London strike the imagination of an untraveled American so much more strongly than those other storied structures, its neighbors, the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody Tower? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire — why, in certain moods, does such a gigantic ghostliness come over the soul at the bare mention of that name, while the thought of Virginia's Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, regardless of all latitudes and longitudes, does the name of the White Sea cast such a spectral spell over the imagination, while that of the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long, lacquered, mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the gaudiest yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a wholly insubstantial example, addressed purely to the imagination, why, in reading the old fairy tales of Central Europe, does "the tall pale man" of the Harz forests, whose changeless pallor glides without a rustle through the green of the groves — why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping imps of the Blocksberg?

It is not entirely the memory of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes, nor the stampedes of her frantic seas, nor the tearlessness of arid skies that never rain, nor the sight of her wide field of leaning spires, wrenched copestones, and crosses all adroop (like the tilted yards of anchored fleets), and her suburban avenues of house-walls lying over upon one another like a tossed pack of cards — it is not these things alone that make tearless Lima the strangest, saddest city you can see. For Lima has taken the white veil, and there is a higher horror in this whiteness of her woe. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins forever new. It does not admit the cheerful greenness of complete decay. It spreads over her broken ramparts the rigid pallor of a stroke that fixes its own distortions.

I know that to ordinary perception, whiteness is not admitted to be the prime agent in heightening the terror of things already terrible. Nor does the unimaginative mind find any terror in those sights whose awfulness, to another mind, consists almost entirely in this one quality — especially when displayed in any form approaching silence or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be clarified by the following examples.

First: The sailor, when approaching foreign coasts, if he hears the roar of breakers at night, snaps to alertness and feels just enough fear to sharpen all his senses. But under exactly the same conditions, let him be called from his hammock to see his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness — as if herds of combed white bears were swimming around him from encircling headlands — and he feels a silent, superstitious dread. The shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is as horrible to him as a real ghost. In vain the sounding lead assures him he is still in deep water. Heart and helm both fail him. He never rests until blue water is beneath him again. Yet where is the sailor who will tell you, "Sir, it was not so much the fear of hitting hidden rocks as the fear of that hideous whiteness that shook me"?

Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes (their peaks capped with snow like the canopied seat on an elephant's back) conveys nothing of dread, except perhaps in merely imagining the eternal frozen desolation that reigns at such vast heights, and the natural thought of how fearful it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same is true of the backwoodsman of the West, who views with comparative indifference a boundless prairie sheeted with driven snow, with no shadow of tree or twig to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas, where at times, by some infernal sleight of hand in the powers of frost and air, he — shivering and half shipwrecked — instead of seeing rainbows that speak hope and comfort to his misery, sees what looks like a boundless churchyard grinning at him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But you say: "I think this white-lead chapter about whiteness is just a white flag hung out by a cowardly soul. You are giving in to a fit of the blues, Ishmael."

Tell me, then — why does a strong young colt, born in some peaceful Vermont valley, far from all predators — why is it that on the sunniest day, if you shake a fresh buffalo hide behind him so he cannot even see it but only smells its wild animal musk — why will he bolt, snort, and paw the ground in frenzy with bulging eyes? He has no memory of being attacked by wild creatures in his green northern home. The strange muskiness cannot remind him of any past danger. What does this New England colt know of the black bison herds of distant Oregon?

Nothing. But here you see, even in a speechless animal, the instinct of knowing the demonic forces in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, when he smells that savage musk, the charging, goring bison herds are as real to him as they are to the abandoned wild foal on the prairies, which at this very moment they may be trampling into dust.

So it is: the muffled rollings of a milky sea, the bleak rustlings of the festooned frosts of mountains, the desolate shiftings of the windrowed snows of prairies — all these are to Ishmael what the shaking of that buffalo robe is to the frightened colt!

Neither the colt nor I knows where the nameless things lie of which the mystic sign gives such hints; yet for me, as for the colt, those things must exist somewhere. Though in many ways this visible world seems to have been made in love, the invisible spheres were made in fright.

But we have not yet solved the spell of this whiteness or learned why it appeals with such power to the soul. And stranger still, far more ominous — why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaningful symbol of spiritual things, the very veil of the Christian's God, and yet at the same time the intensifying agent in things most appalling to humanity.

Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and so stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation when we gaze into the white depths of the Milky Way? Or is it that whiteness, in its essence, is not so much a color as the visible absence of color, and at the same time the concrete of all colors? Is it for these reasons that there is such a dumb blankness, full of meaning, in a wide landscape of snows — a colorless all-color of atheism from which we shrink? And when we consider that other theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly hues — every stately or lovely emblazoning, the sweet tinges of sunset skies and woods, yes, and the gilded velvets of butterflies, and the butterfly cheeks of young girls — all these are only subtle deceits, not actually inherent in substances, but only laid on from outside; so that all deified Nature absolutely paints like the harlot, whose allurements cover nothing but the charnel-house within; and when we go further and consider that the mystical cosmetic that produces every one of her hues, the great principle of light, forever remains white or colorless in itself, and if it acted upon matter without a medium, would touch all objects, even tulips and roses, with its own blank tinge — pondering all this, the palsied universe lies before us a leper. And like willful travelers in Lapland who refuse to wear colored and coloring glasses over their eyes, so the wretched infidel gazes himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps the whole prospect around him. And of all these things the albino whale was the symbol. Do you wonder, then, at the fiery hunt?

modern_da.title: Kapitel 42 — Hvalens Hvidhed
paragraphs: Hvad den hvide hval betød for Ahab, er blevet antydet. Hvad han til tider var for mig, er stadig usagt.

Ud over de mere åbenlyse rædsler, som Moby Dick kunne vække i enhver mands sjæl, var der en anden tanke — eller rettere en vag, unævnelig gru ved ham — som til tider overvældede alt andet med sin styrke. Men den var så mystisk, så næsten umulig at sætte ord på, at jeg næsten opgiver at gøre den forståelig. Det var hvalens hvidhed, der forfærdede mig mere end noget andet. Men hvordan kan jeg håbe på at forklare mig her? Og alligevel, på en dunkel, famlende måde må jeg forklare mig, ellers vil alle disse kapitler have været forgæves.

I mange naturlige ting forfiner og forhøjer hvidheden skønheden, som om den gav den en særlig dyd af sin egen — som i marmor, japonicaer og perler. Forskellige nationer har på en eller anden måde anerkendt en vis kongelig fortrinsstilling hos denne farve. Pegus barbariske, store gamle konger satte titlen »Herre over de Hvide Elefanter« over alle deres andre højtravende herredømmetitler. Siams moderne konger hejste det samme snehvide dyr på deres kongelige banner. Det hannoveranske flag bar den ene skikkelse af en snehvid stridshest. Det store østrigske kejserrige, cæsarisk arving til det overherskende Rom, tog den samme kejserlige farve til sin kejserlige farve. Denne fortrinsstilling gælder selve menneskeslægten og giver den hvide mand ideelt herredømme over enhver mørk stamme. Ud over alt dette er hvidheden endda gjort til tegn på glæde — hos romerne markerede en hvid sten en glædelig dag. I andre menneskelige sympatier og symboler er den samme farve gjort til sindbillede på mange rørende, ædle ting: brudes uskyld, alderdommens venlighed. Blandt Amerikas rødhuder var gaven af det hvide bælte af wampum det dybeste æresløfte. I mange lande står hvidhed for retfærdighedens majestæt i dommerens hermelin og føjer til den daglige pragt hos konger og dronninger, der trækkes af mælkehvide heste. Selv i de højere mysterier i de mest ophøjede religioner er den gjort til symbol på guddommelig renhed og magt. De persiske ildtilbedere holdt den hvide gaffelformede flamme for den helligste på alteret. I de græske mytologier blev selve den store Jupiter inkarneret i en snehvid tyr. Blandt de ædle irokesere var midvinteroffret af den hellige Hvide Hund langt den helligste fest i deres teologi — den pletfri, trofaste skabning blev anset for det reneste sendebud, de kunne sende til Den Store Ånd med den årlige nyhed om deres egen trofasthed. Direkte fra det latinske ord for hvid udleder alle kristne præster navnet på en del af deres hellige dragt — albaen, tunikaen, der bæres under sutanen. Blandt den romerske kirkes hellige ceremonier bruges hvidt særligt ved fejringen af vor Herres lidelse. I Johannes' syn gives de frelste hvide klæder, og de fireogtyve ældste står klædt i hvidt foran den store hvide trone, og Den Hellige, der sidder på den, er hvid som uld. Men trods alle disse ophobede forbindelser med alt, hvad der er sødt, hæderligt og ophøjet, lurer der stadig noget uhåndgribeligt i den inderste idé om denne farve, som slår mere panik ind i sjælen end det røde, der skræmmer os i blodet.

Det er denne uhåndgribelige egenskab, der får tanken om hvidhed, når den adskilles fra venligere forbindelser og forenes med en genstand, der i sig selv er frygtelig, til at drive rædslen op til det yderste. Tænk på polernes hvide bjørn og tropernes hvide haj. Hvad andet end deres glatte, flagede hvidhed gør dem til de overjordiske rædsler, de er? Det er den spøgelsesagtige hvidhed, der giver deres blik, når de stirrer stumt og grådigt, en så afskyelig mildhed, endnu mere væmmelig end skræmmende. Så ikke engang den hugtandede tiger i sin heraldiske pels kan forvirre modet så meget som den hvidsvøbte bjørn eller haj.*

*Med hensyn til isbjørnen kan det muligvis hævdes af enhver, der vil gå endnu dybere ind i sagen, at det ikke er hvidheden, betragtet for sig selv, der forøger dyrets uudholdelige hæslighed. For når man analyserer den forøgede hæslighed, kunne man sige, opstår den kun af, at skabningens uansvarlige vildskab er klædt i den himmelske uskylds og kærligheds uld; og ved at bringe to så modsatte følelser sammen i vores sind skræmmer isbjørnen os med en så unaturlig kontrast. Men selv hvis alt dette er sandt, ville man ikke få den forøgede rædsel, hvis det ikke var for hvidheden.

Hvad den hvide haj angår, svarer den hvide, glidende spøgelsesagtighed hos den skabning, når den hviler og ses i sit almindelige humør, mærkeligt til den samme egenskab hos den nordlige firbenede. Franskmændene rammer denne ejendommelighed mest levende i det navn, de giver den fisk. Den romerske kirkes messe for de døde begynder med »Requiem eternam« (evig hvile), og herfra har »Requiem« navnet på selve messen og enhver anden begravelsesmusik. Nu kalder franskmændene den Requin, med hentydning til dødens hvide, tavse stilhed hos denne haj og den milde dødelighed i dens vaner.

Tænk på albatrossen. Hvor kommer de skyer af åndeligt under og bleg gru fra, hvori det hvide fantom sejler i enhver fantasi? Det var ikke Coleridge, der først kastede den trolddom, men Guds store, uskønmalende hofdigter, Naturen.*

*Jeg husker den første albatros, jeg nogensinde så. Det var under en langvarig storm i farvand tæt på de antarktiske have. Fra min morgenvagt nedenunder gik jeg op på det overskyede dæk. Der, slynget ned på storlugerne, så jeg et kongeligt, fjerklædt væsen af pletfri hvidhed med et krumt, romersk næb, ophøjet. Med mellemrum bøjede den sine vældige ærkeenglevinger, som for at omfavne en hellig ark. Vidunderlige flagren og bæven rystede den. Skønt dens krop var uskadt, udstødte den skrig som en konges genfærd i overnaturlig nød. Gennem dens ubeskrivelige, mærkelige øjne troede jeg at skimte hemmeligheder, der berørte Gud. Som Abraham for englene bøjede jeg mig. Det hvide væsen var så hvidt, dets vinger så brede, og i de for evigt landflygtige farvande havde jeg mistet de elendige, fordrejende erindringer om traditioner og byer. Længe stirrede jeg på det vidunder af fjerdragt. Jeg kan ikke sige — jeg kan kun antyde — de ting, der fór gennem mig dengang. Men til sidst kom jeg til mig selv, og jeg vendte mig om og spurgte en sømand, hvilken fugl det var. En goney, svarede han. Goney! Det navn havde jeg aldrig hørt før. Er det tænkeligt, at dette herlige væsen er helt ukendt for folk i land? Aldrig! Men nogen tid efter fandt jeg ud af, at »goney« var sømandens navn for albatrossen. Så Coleridges vilde Rhyme kan umuligt have haft noget med mine mystiske indtryk at gøre, da jeg så den fugl på vores dæk. For jeg havde dengang ikke læst Rhyme, og jeg vidste heller ikke, at fuglen var en albatros. Alligevel polerer jeg ved at sige dette kun indirekte digtets og digterens ædle fortjeneste en smule blankere.

Jeg fastholder altså, at fortryllelsens hemmelighed hovedsagelig lurer i fuglens vidunderlige kropslige hvidhed. Denne sandhed er så meget desto tydeligere, når man tænker på, at der — i en selvmodsigelse — findes fugle, der kaldes grå albatrosser. Dem har jeg ofte set, men aldrig med sådanne følelser som dengang, jeg så den antarktiske fugl.

Men hvordan var det mystiske væsen blevet fanget? Sig ikke et ord, så skal jeg fortælle det: med en forræderisk krog og line, mens fuglen flød på havet. Til sidst gjorde kaptajnen den til postbud, ved at binde en læderlap med påskrift om skibets tid og sted om dens hals og så lade den undslippe. Men jeg tvivler ikke på, at læderlappen, der var beregnet til mennesker, blev taget af i Himlen, da den hvide fugl fløj op for at slutte sig til de vingefoldende, påkaldende og tilbedende keruber!

Mest berømt i vores vestlige annaler og indianske overleveringer er Prærienes Hvide Hingst — en strålende mælkehvid stridshest, storøjet, småhovedet, bredbrystet, med tusind monarkers værdighed i sin ophøjede, foragtfulde holdning. Han var den valgte Xerxes over vældige flokke af vilde heste, hvis græsgange i de dage kun var indhegnet af Klippebjergene og Alleghenybjergene. I spidsen for dem drog han mod vest som den udvalgte stjerne, der hver aften fører lysets hære an. Hans manes funklende vandfald og halens krumme komet pyntede ham i en pragt mere strålende, end guld- og sølvslagere kunne have skaffet. Han var et mest kejserligt og ærkeenglelignende syn fra den ufaldne vestlige verden, som for de gamle fangstmænds og jægeres øjne genoplivede herligheden fra de oldtidstider, da Adam gik majestætisk som en gud, med åben pande og uforfærdet som denne mægtige hingst. Hvad enten han marcherede blandt sine adjudanter og marskaller i spidsen for utallige kolonner, der strømmede uendeligt hen over sletterne som en Ohio, eller han med sine undersåtter, der græssede rundt om ham til horisonten, holdt revy over dem i galop, mens hans varme næsebor rødmede gennem hans kølige mælkehvidhed — i hvilken skikkelse han end viste sig, var han altid genstand for skælvende ærefrygt og forundring hos de tapreste indianere. Og det kan heller ikke betvivles, ud fra hvad der står på legendarisk optegnelse om denne ædle hest, at det hovedsagelig var hans åndelige hvidhed, der klædte ham så i guddommelighed; og at denne guddommelighed havde noget i sig, som, skønt den bød tilbedelse, samtidig påtvang en vis unævnelig rædsel.
Men der er andre tilfælde, hvor hvidheden mister al den ekstra fremmede herlighed, den har i Den Hvide Hingst og Albatrossen.

Hvad er det ved albinoen, der så særligt støder og ofte chokerer øjet, så han nogle gange endda foragtes af sin egen familie? Det er hvidheden, der dækker ham, netop det, hans navn udtrykker. Albinoen er lige så velbygget som andre mænd — han har ingen egentlig misdannelse — og alligevel gør denne altomsluttende hvidhed ham mere uhyggeligt afskyelig end den styggeste misfødsel (en vansiret, uhyrlig fødsel). Hvorfor skulle det være sådan?

Heller ikke i helt andre skikkelser undlader Naturen, i sine mindst håndgribelige men ikke mindre ondsindede gerninger, at kalde denne højeste egenskab ved det rædselsfulde ind blandt sine kræfter. På grund af dets snehvide udseende er det panserhandskeklædte spøgelse i Sydhavet blevet kaldt den Hvide Byge. Heller ikke i nogle historiske tilfælde har menneskelig ondskabs kunst undværet en så mægtig forbundsfælle. Hvor vildt den forstærker virkningen af den passage hos Froissart, hvor Gents desperate Hvide Hætter, maskerede i deres partis snehvide symbol, myrder deres foged på torvet!

I visse ting vidner hele menneskehedens fælles, nedarvede erfaring om denne farves overnaturlige kraft. Det kan næppe betvivles, at den eneste synlige egenskab ved de døde, der forfærder den, der ser på dem, mest, er den marmorbleghed, der bliver ved at ligge over dem — som om den bleghed var lige så meget et tegn på rædsel i den næste verden, som den er på dødsangst i denne. Fra de dødes bleghed låner vi farven på ligklædet, vi svøber dem i. Selv i vores overtro kaster vi den samme snehvide kappe om vore spøgelser — alle genfærd stiger op i en mælkehvid tåge. Og mens disse rædsler holder os i deres greb, lad os føje til, at selv rædslernes konge, som evangelisten skildrer ham, rider på en bleg hest.

Hvad stort eller yndefuldt et menneske end i andre stemninger kan lade hvidheden stå for, kan ingen derfor benægte, at den i sin dybeste, mest idealiserede betydning kalder et ejendommeligt genfærd frem i sjælen.

Men selv om dette punkt er afgjort uden for enhver tvivl, hvordan kan nogen dødelig så forklare det? At analysere det synes umuligt. Kan vi så håbe at støde på et fingerpeg, der fører os til den skjulte årsag, vi søger, ved at anføre nogle af de tilfælde, hvor denne hvidhed — selv om den i øjeblikket for det meste eller helt er renset for alle direkte forbindelser, der kunne give den noget frygtindgydende — alligevel viser sig at øve den samme trolddom over os, om end i svækket form?

Lad os prøve. Men i en sag som denne taler det fine til det fine, og uden fantasi kan ingen følge nogen anden ind i disse haller. Og selv om i hvert fald nogle af de fantasifulde indtryk, jeg nu vil fremlægge, uden tvivl er blevet delt af de fleste mennesker, har få måske været sig dem fuldt bevidst dengang, og derfor kan de ikke kalde dem frem nu.

Hvorfor kalder blot ordet pinse (kirkeårets pinsetid) hos den mand med ukultiveret fantasi, der kun løseligt kender dagens særlige præg, sådanne lange, dystre, tavse optog af langsomt skridtende pilgrimme frem, nedslåede og iklædt hætter af nyfaldet sne? Eller hvorfor vækker blot det at høre en Hvid Broder eller en Hvid Nonne nævnt en så øjenløs statue i sjælen hos den ulærde, ukomplicerede protestant fra de mellemste amerikanske stater?

Eller hvad er det — bortset fra beretningerne om fængslede krigere og konger, som ikke helt kan forklare det — der gør, at Det Hvide Tårn i London griber en rejseuvant amerikaners fantasi så meget stærkere end de andre sagnomspundne bygninger, dets naboer, Byward-tårnet eller endda Det Blodige Tårn? Og de mere ophøjede tårne, New Hampshires Hvide Bjerge — hvorfor kommer der i visse stemninger sådan en kæmpemæssig spøgelsesagtighed over sjælen ved blot at høre det navn, mens tanken om Virginias Blue Ridge er fuld af en blød, dugfrisk, fjern drømmeagtighed? Eller hvorfor kaster Det Hvide Hav, uanset alle bredde- og længdegrader, sådan en spøgelsesagtig trolddom over fantasien, mens Det Gule Hav vugger os med dødelige tanker om lange, lakerede, milde eftermiddage på bølgerne, efterfulgt af de mest prangende og søvnigste solnedgange? Eller, for at tage et helt uhåndgribeligt eksempel, rettet alene til fantasien: Hvorfor er »den høje, blege mand« fra Harzens skove i de gamle eventyr fra Mellemeuropa, hvis uforanderlige bleghed glider uden en raslen gennem lundenes grønne — hvorfor er dette genfærd mere frygteligt end alle Blocksbergs skrigende smådjævle?

Det er ikke helt mindet om hendes katedralstyrtende jordskælv, ikke hendes vanvittige havs stormløb, ikke de tørre himles tårefrihed, der aldrig regner, og heller ikke synet af hendes vide mark af skæve spir, vredne kronesten og nedhængende kors (som de skæve rår på ankrede flåder) og hendes forstadsalleer af husmure, der ligger hen over hinanden som et kastet spil kort — det er ikke disse ting alene, der gør tårefri Lima til den sælsomste, tristeste by, man kan se. For Lima har taget det hvide slør, og der er en højere gru i denne hvidhed i hendes sorg. Gammel som Pizarro holder denne hvidhed hendes ruiner evigt nye. Den tillader ikke den muntre grønhed ved fuldstændigt forfald. Den breder hen over hendes knækkede volde en stiv bleghed, som et slagtilfælde, der gør sine egne fordrejninger faste.

Jeg ved, at for almindelig opfattelse regnes hvidheden ikke for det vigtigste middel til at forøge rædslen ved ting, der i forvejen er rædselsfulde. Og det fantasiløse sind finder heller ikke nogen rædsel i de syn, hvis forfærdelighed for et andet sind næsten helt består i denne ene egenskab — især når den vises i en form, der nærmer sig stilhed eller almenhed. Hvad jeg mener med de to udsagn, kan måske klares ved de følgende eksempler.

Først: Når søfarenden nærmer sig fremmede kyster og om natten hører brændingens brøl, vågner han til opmærksomhed og føler netop så megen frygt, som der skal til for at skærpe alle hans sanser. Men under helt de samme forhold, lad ham så blive kaldt op af sin hængekøje for at se sit skib sejle gennem et midnatshav af mælkehvidhed — som om flokke af kæmmede hvide bjørne svømmede rundt om ham fra omkransende forbjerge — og han føler en tavs, overtroisk gru. Det indhyllede genfærd fra de hvidnede vande er lige så skrækkeligt for ham som et ægte spøgelse. Forgæves forsikrer lodblyet ham om, at han stadig er på dybt vand. Hjerte og ror svigter ham begge. Han hviler aldrig, før der igen er blåt vand under ham. Alligevel, hvor er den sømand, der vil sige til dig: »Sir, det var ikke så meget frygten for at ramme skjulte klipper, som frygten for den afskyelige hvidhed, der rystede mig«?

For det andet: For den indfødte indianer i Peru bringer det evige syn af de sne-baldakinerede Andesbjerge (deres tinder dækket af sne som det overdækkede sæde på en elefants ryg) intet med sig af frygt, undtagen måske når han blot forestiller sig den evige frosne øde, der hersker i sådanne enorme højder, og den naturlige tanke om, hvor frygteligt det ville være at fare vild i sådanne umenneskelige ensomheder. Det samme gælder nogenlunde for vestens bygdemand, der med forholdsvis ligegyldighed betragter en grænseløs prærie, dækket af drevet sne, uden en skygge af træ eller kvist til at bryde hvidhedens faste trance. Ikke sådan med sømanden, når han ser landskabet i de antarktiske have, hvor han til tider, ved en helvedes fingerfærdighed i frostens og luftens kræfter, skælvende og halvt forlist, i stedet for at se regnbuer, der taler om håb og trøst i hans elendighed, ser noget, der ligner en grænseløs kirkegård, der griner ad ham med sine magre ismonumenter og splintrede kors.
Men du siger: »Jeg synes, dette hvidtblykapitel om hvidhed bare er et hvidt flag, hængt ud af en fejg sjæl. Du giver efter for et anfald af tungsind, Ishmael.«

Sig mig så — hvorfor kan et stærkt ungt føl, født i en fredfyldt dal i Vermont, langt fra alle rovdyr — hvorfor er det, at hvis man på den solrigeste dag ryster en frisk bøffelhud bag ham, så han slet ikke kan se den, men kun lugter dens vilde dyremusk — hvorfor vil han så fare op, pruste og skrabe jorden i vildskab med udstående øjne? Han har ingen erindring om at være blevet angrebet af vilde dyr i sit grønne nordlige hjem. Den fremmede moskusduft kan ikke minde ham om nogen fare i fortiden. Hvad ved dette føl fra New England om de sorte bisonokser i det fjerne Oregon?

Intet. Men her ser du, selv hos et stumt dyr, instinktet til at kende de dæmoniske kræfter i verden. Selv om det er tusinder af engelske mil fra Oregon, er de stormende, stangende bisonhjorde lige så virkelige for ham, når han lugter den vilde moskus, som de er for det forladte vilde føl på prærierne, som de netop i dette øjeblik måske tramper til støv.

Sådan er det: det dæmpede rullen i et mælkehvidt hav, den triste raslen i bjergenes festonerede frost, de øde forskydninger i prærienes vindbankede sne — alt dette er for Ishmael, hvad rystelsen af bøffelskindet er for det forskrækkede føl!

Hverken følet eller jeg ved, hvor de navnløse ting ligger, som det mystiske tegn giver sådanne antydninger om; og dog må de ting for mig, som for følet, findes et sted. Selv om denne synlige verden på mange måder synes at være skabt i kærlighed, er de usynlige sfærer skabt i skræk.

Men vi har endnu ikke løst trolddommen i denne hvidhed eller lært, hvorfor den taler så stærkt til sjælen. Og mere mærkeligt, langt mere uheldsvangert — hvorfor den, som vi har set, på én gang er det mest betydningsfulde symbol på åndelige ting, selve den kristnes Guds slør, og alligevel samtidig det, der forstærker de ting, der skræmmer menneskeheden mest.

Er det, fordi den ved sin ubestemthed skyggelægger universets hjerteløse tomrum og uhyre vidder og således stikker os i ryggen med tanken om udslettelse, når vi stirrer ind i Mælkevejens hvide dyb? Eller er det, fordi hvidhed i sit væsen ikke så meget er en farve som den synlige mangel på farve, og samtidig summen af alle farver? Er det af disse grunde, at der er sådan en stum tomhed, fuld af mening, i et vidt landskab af sne — en farveløs alfarve af ateisme, som vi viger tilbage for? Og når vi tænker på den anden teori hos naturfilosofferne, at alle andre jordiske farver — enhver statelig eller yndig udsmykning, solnedgangshimlenes og skovenes søde nuancer, ja, og sommerfuglenes forgyldte fløjl og unge pigers sommerfuglekinder — alle er kun snedige bedrag, der ikke egentlig hører til tingene, men kun er lagt udenpå; så al den guddommeliggjorte Natur ganske simpelt maler sig som skøgen, hvis lokkemidler ikke dækker over andet end ligkælderen indeni; og når vi går videre og tænker på, at den mystiske sminke, der frembringer hver eneste af hendes farver, lysets store princip, for evigt forbliver hvidt eller farveløst i sig selv, og hvis det virkede på stoffet uden et mellemled, ville berøre alle ting, selv tulipaner og roser, med sin egen tomme farvetone — når vi grubler over alt dette, ligger det lammede univers foran os som en spedalsk. Og som egensindige rejsende i Lapland, der nægter at bære farvede og farvegivende briller for øjnene, således stirrer den elendige vantro sig blind på det monumentale hvide ligklæde, der svøber hele udsigten omkring ham. Og af alle disse ting var albinohvalen symbolet. Undrer du dig da over den brændende jagt?
